## 1. A problematic simulation example

This is a saved example from the RCC v5 pilot: a 2 Mb locus with 3,508 variants,
200,000 study individuals, and 5,000 reference individuals. The populations split
200 generations ago. There is one causal variant (SNP 729), and regional
heritability is 0.3%. Recombination is $10^{-8}$ per base per generation.
We load the original LD matrices and association statistics without resimulating.
All SNP indices below use R's one-based indexing.

```{r}
library(susieRobust)
library(susieR)
# The prior-variance plot uses the trace$effect format in susieR 0.16.6.

example <- readRDS("data/problematic-simulation/example.rds")
R <- readRDS("data/problematic-simulation/R.rds")
R0 <- readRDS("data/problematic-simulation/R0.rds")
v <- example$v
N <- example$N; causal <- example$causal; J <- length(v)
L_max <- 10L; max_iter <- 100L; tol <- 1e-4
coverage <- 0.95; min_abs_corr <- 0.5
```

### Three linearly dependent variants

SNPs 588, 597, and 600 are linearly dependent in the reference panel. Their
$3\times3$ reference LD matrix has a zero eigenvalue, even though no pair is
perfectly correlated. If $a$ is its unit null eigenvector, then
$R_{0,\gamma}a=0$, but $a^\top v_\gamma\ne0$: the association statistics do not
respect the reference panel's linear dependence. The corresponding in-sample
LD block does not have this exact dependence.

```{r}
gamma <- c(588L, 597L, 600L)
round(R0[gamma, gamma], 4)
e <- eigen(R0[gamma, gamma], symmetric=TRUE)
a <- e$vectors[, which.min(e$values)]
if (a[2] < 0) a <- -a  # Fix the arbitrary eigenvector sign.
data.frame(SNP=gamma, null_direction=a, v=v[gamma])
data.frame(
  reference_min_eigenvalue=min(e$values),
  in_sample_min_eigenvalue=min(eigen(R[gamma, gamma], symmetric=TRUE)$values),
  reference_null_residual=sqrt(sum((R0[, gamma] %*% a)^2)),
  association_null_contrast=sum(a * v[gamma])
)
```

Along this direction, the RSS likelihood can favor large opposing effects.
A small ridge makes the matrix invertible, but leaves a weakly penalized
direction and can lead to slow updates. Here we use the same ridge,
$10^{-4}$, for both in-sample and reference RSS, learn the effect prior
variances, and keep the residual variance fixed at 1.

```{r}
ridge <- 1e-4
fit_in_sample <- susieR::susie_ss(
  XtX=N * ((1-ridge)*R + ridge*diag(J)), Xty=N*v, yty=N, n=N,
  L=L_max, standardize=FALSE, residual_variance=1,
  estimate_residual_variance=FALSE, estimate_prior_variance=TRUE,
  scaled_prior_variance=0.2, check_prior=FALSE,
  max_iter=max_iter, tol=tol, coverage=coverage,
  min_abs_corr=min_abs_corr, n_purity=J, track_fit=TRUE)

fit_reference <- susieR::susie_ss(
  XtX=N * ((1-ridge)*R0 + ridge*diag(J)), Xty=N*v, yty=N, n=N,
  L=L_max, standardize=FALSE, residual_variance=1,
  estimate_residual_variance=FALSE, estimate_prior_variance=TRUE,
  scaled_prior_variance=0.2, check_prior=FALSE,
  max_iter=max_iter, tol=tol, coverage=coverage,
  min_abs_corr=min_abs_corr, n_purity=J, track_fit=TRUE)

data.frame(
  LD=c("In-sample", "Reference"),
  iterations=c(fit_in_sample$niter, fit_reference$niter),
  converged=c(fit_in_sample$converged, fit_reference$converged),
  causal_PIP=c(fit_in_sample$pip[causal], fit_reference$pip[causal])
)
```

The causal SNP is marked in red in the PIP plots.

```{r rss-pips, fig.width=10, fig.height=4}
par(mfrow=c(1,2))
plot_pip(fit_in_sample, causal=causal, R=R, main="In-sample RSS: L = 10")
plot_pip(fit_reference, causal=causal, R=R0, main="Reference RSS: L = 10")
par(mfrow=c(1,1))
```

Each curve below is the learned prior variance of one single-effect component.
Iteration 0 is the initialization. The in-sample trace ends when its fit stops.

```{r prior-variance, fig.width=10, fig.height=4}
par(mfrow=c(1,2))
for (name in c("In-sample", "Reference")) {
  fit <- if (name == "In-sample") fit_in_sample else fit_reference
  history <- fit$trace$effect
  V <- with(history, tapply(V, list(iteration, effect), identity))
  matplot(as.numeric(rownames(V)), V, type="l", lty=1,
          xlab="Iteration", ylab="Learned prior variance",
          main=paste(name, "RSS: L = 10"))
}
par(mfrow=c(1,1))
```

## 2. AIW with 100 iteration cap

Now restrict AIW to $L=1,\ldots,5$, keeping the same 100-iteration cap and
RSS convergence tolerance. All candidate fits start from fresh initialization.

```{r}
set.seed(example$seed)
time_aiw <- system.time(fit_aiw <- susie_aiw(
  v=v, R0=R0, N=N, L=1:5, max_iter=100, tol=1e-4,
  rss_ridge=1e-4, estimate_prior_variance=TRUE,
  lambda_max = .1,
  keep_fits=TRUE))["elapsed"]

fit_aiw$scores[, c("L", "objective", "rss_iterations", "rss_converged",
                   "rss_last_elbo_change", "selected")]
```

```{r aiw-small-ridge, fig.width=10, fig.height=4}
par(mfrow=c(1,2))
plot(fit_aiw$scores$L, fit_aiw$scores$objective, type="b", pch=16,
     xlab="Candidate L", ylab="AIW score", main="Ridge = 1e-4")
abline(v=fit_aiw$selected_L, col="red", lty=2)
plot_pip(fit_aiw, causal=causal, R=R0,
         main=paste("AIW-selected RSS: L =", fit_aiw$selected_L))
par(mfrow=c(1,1))
```

The convergence problem is still present among the candidate RSS fits, but
AIW selects $L=`r fit_aiw$selected_L`$, whose RSS fit did converge.
Convergence does not guarantee perfect fine-mapping: inspect the selected
credible sets below, including whether they contain the true causal SNP.

```{r}
data.frame(CS=names(fit_aiw$sets$cs), size=lengths(fit_aiw$sets$cs),
           contains_causal=sapply(fit_aiw$sets$cs, function(s) any(causal %in% s)))
```

## 3. AIW with a 1,000-iteration cap

Increase only the iteration cap from 100 to 1,000. Keep $L=1,\ldots,5$,
`rss_ridge = 1e-4`, and all other settings the same as in section 2.

```{r}
set.seed(example$seed)
time_aiw_1000 <- system.time(fit_aiw_1000 <- susie_aiw(
  v=v, R0=R0, N=N, L=1:5, max_iter=1000, tol=1e-4,
  rss_ridge=1e-4, estimate_prior_variance=TRUE,
  lambda_max = .1,
  keep_fits=TRUE))["elapsed"]

fit_aiw_1000$scores[, c("L", "objective", "rss_iterations", "rss_converged",
                       "rss_last_elbo_change", "selected")]
```

```{r aiw-1000-iterations, fig.width=10, fig.height=4}
par(mfrow=c(1,2))
plot(fit_aiw_1000$scores$L, fit_aiw_1000$scores$objective,
     type="b", pch=16, xlab="Candidate L", ylab="AIW score", main="Iteration cap = 1000")
abline(v=fit_aiw_1000$selected_L, col="red", lty=2)
plot_pip(fit_aiw_1000, causal=causal, R=R0,
         main=paste("AIW-selected RSS: L =", fit_aiw_1000$selected_L))
par(mfrow=c(1,1))
```

```{r}
selected_100 <- subset(fit_aiw$scores, selected)
selected_1000 <- subset(fit_aiw_1000$scores, selected)
data.frame(
  iteration_cap=c(100, 1000),
  elapsed_seconds=c(unname(time_aiw), unname(time_aiw_1000)),
  selected_L=c(fit_aiw$selected_L, fit_aiw_1000$selected_L),
  selected_RSS_iterations=c(selected_100$rss_iterations, selected_1000$rss_iterations),
  selected_RSS_converged=c(selected_100$rss_converged, selected_1000$rss_converged)
)
data.frame(
  max_PIP_difference=max(abs(fit_aiw$pip - fit_aiw_1000$pip)),
  identical_credible_sets=identical(fit_aiw$sets$cs, fit_aiw_1000$sets$cs)
)
```

The RSS fit at the AIW-selected $L=`r fit_aiw_1000$selected_L`$ converges in
only `r selected_1000$rss_iterations` iterations, well below either cap.
Increasing the cap makes the overall algorithm slower because the larger,
nonconverged candidates continue running. It does not change the selected
$L$, PIPs, or credible sets in this example. The scores of the nonselected
candidates do change as their RSS fits continue to update.
